Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
abstract: Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses . Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware. Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware. Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does. Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side. We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS. The Impact of Fragmentation Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux. The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation. The Stack and the macOS Gaps Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time . To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support. Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three. The Cuttlefish-on-Mac stack. Cuttlefish orchestrates virtual devices backed by QEMU. The highlighted orange blocks are the Mac-specific work: adding macOS support to vhost-user, increasing memory-region tracking slots in QEMU’s HVF backend, and using the native Cocoa display and code-signing paths. Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user , and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux. title: Production MLOps at GS Caltex with Amazon SageMaker Canvas, part 1
abstract: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. Solution overview The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. From a validated model to a repeatable workflow You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform , and stores the results in S3. title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
abstract: Coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI work in tasks. A developer asks for a change, and the agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests until the work is done. One task can take a few model calls or dozens. What the developer pays for is the task, not one call. The price per token alone doesn’t tell you what a whole task costs. The total depends on how many turns a model needs, how much history each turn replays, and how often a task has to be retried or never finishes. You pay for every attempt, including attempts on tasks that never finish. So when you route a coding agent’s requests between models, judge the routing by cost per solved task: the total cost of your runs divided by the number of runs whose tests pass. NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard is an open source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. You define the models that it can use and the strategy that it follows. Its LiteLLM integration supports two strategies. Stage routing reads the recent tool activity and results in the request history, and then picks one of two candidate models. Random routing picks from the configured models, with optional weights, for traffic splits and A/B comparisons. Another option you can explore is LiteLLM, who also recently shipped a native built-in Switchyard stage router as an auto-router strategy. In this post, you use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy LiteLLM, an open source gateway for large language models (LLMs), with the Switchyard routing plugin in your AWS account. LiteLLM calls the models on Amazon Bedrock . You then use the sample’s benchmark runners to measure cost per solved task for a routed model group and for single-model baseline groups, so that you can evaluate routing against your own workloads. Note: The sample installs switchyard-server 0.3.0 from crates.io and runs the published LiteLLM v1.102.0 image. NVIDIA documents switchyard-server 0.3.0 as a demo and evaluation component, and its configuration can change between releases. This sample uses the experimental Switchyard LiteLLM integration and its configuration and APIs may change between releases. This is sample code, for non-production usage. Work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before deployment. Deploy the sample in a non-production account and test it before relying on it. Solution overview Figure 1 shows the architecture of the solution. LiteLLM and the Switchyard plugin run in one container image on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate , in private subnets. Figure 1: Solution architecture A request flows through these steps. The numbers match the diagram. The coding agent sends an OpenAI-compatible request with the model field set to switchyard , the LiteLLM model group that Switchyard routes, and the shared gateway key in the Authorization header. The endpoint is your hostname over HTTPS, with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate on the load balancer, and only the IPv4 CIDR range that you allow can reach it. With a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53 , Route 53 resolves the hostname to the load balancer. AWS WAF filters the request with IP reputation, known bad input, and per-IP rate-limit rules. The Application Load Balancer forwards only /v1/chat/completions , /v1/models , and /health/liveliness to the ECS task in a private subnet, and answers every other path with 404. The task runs one container: LiteLLM with the embedded Switchyard plugin. LiteLLM validates the gateway key and calls the plugin to pick a model. Stage chooses between a capable model and a lower-cost efficient model. It reads the tool activity and results in the request history, so the agent must send the full conversation history. title: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
abstract: Agents today review code, process claims, and run unattended for hours. Many also sit behind interactive experiences where a person waits for the first response. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime gives these agents a fully managed, serverless environment: each session runs in its own isolated microVM, the platform scales to zero when there’s no work, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume. AgentCore runtime with platformVersion set to “V2” changes how sessions start. Instead of initializing your container for every session, it prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores that snapshot for each new session. Session start times are faster and more consistent. V2 also reclaims memory your sessions don’t use, so your bill tracks what your agent uses. For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes. Some agents need restructuring to get the full benefit, and for chat and voice experiences even 2 seconds is too slow. This post explains how V2 starts a session, how to measure session start time, and how to keep work off the first request, including build hooks, which AgentCore runtime now supports. We cover four patterns, from changes to your agent’s code to starting sessions before users need them. Which pattern do you need? Your situation What to do Section A new session in about 2 seconds is fine Switch to V2 and do all initialization before app.run() Keep work off the first request Your agent needs large files, a CLI, or a browser early, and can’t hold them in its process Add a build hook to load and prime them while the snapshot is built Working with hooks You need sub-second, and users engage before they send their first request (opening the app or a chat window) Start the session in the background when the user engages Pre-warm on user engagement How V2 starts a session AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM. On V1, AgentCore pulls your container image from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), starts the container, and runs your initialization code before it can process the first request. The image pull dominates, so cold start grows with image size. V2 does that work once. When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore runtime starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping ( GET /ping ), which must arrive within 120 seconds. It then clears the operating system’s file cache, to keep the snapshot small, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot. This is a change from V1: Every create or update now takes a few minutes while the snapshot is built. In this post, init means everything your agent does before /ping reports healthy. With the AgentCore Python SDK, that’s everything before app.run() . If you run your own HTTP server, in Node.js or another language, report healthy only after your initialization finishes. Figure 1: Build, once per create or update When a new session arrives, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM. Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with its imports, objects, and clients in place. Files from your image are loaded lazily: each block is fetched the first time a session reads it. Figure 2: Invoke, every new session Three facts follow from these flows, and the rest of this post builds on them: Memory comes back whole. Anything your process held at snapshot time, and anything in a RAM-backed file system such as /dev/shm , is available at memory speed from the first access. File reads don’t carry over. The file cache is cleared before the freeze, so reading a file during init doesn’t make it fast in a restored session. Image files are fetched on first read. The first read of a block comes from snapshot storage and is then cached closer to the host. title: OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures
abstract: You can deploy OpenFold3-preview from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . The OpenFold Consortium and the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University developed OpenFold3 as an open source biomolecular structure prediction model. With a few lines of code, you can typically deploy OpenFold3 into your own AWS account. You can then predict the 3D structures of proteins, DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, and the complexes they form. The endpoint runs with network isolation, which you can use to help keep your sequences within your AWS account. Computational drug discovery teams now use structure prediction as a core part of their work. Teams use it in target identification, antibody and protein engineering, and structure-based virtual screening. Teams have found running these models challenging. You need GPU infrastructure, a working CUDA and PyTorch stack, large model checkpoints, and a serving layer that handles requests that take minutes rather than milliseconds. SageMaker JumpStart can handle much of that work for you. OpenFold3 runs in an AWS-maintained container on a managed Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint. The endpoint is designed to handle request queuing and GPU warmup, and you can add autoscaling. In this post, we show you how to: Deploy OpenFold3-preview on a SageMaker asynchronous inference endpoint. Submit structure prediction jobs and interpret the results, including predicted structures and confidence scores. Run several predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances . Supply your own multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to improve prediction accuracy while helping keep your sequences private. Help reduce costs by scaling your endpoint to zero when it’s idle. Overview of OpenFold3 OpenFold3 is an all-atom structure prediction model. It predicts the joint 3D structure of a set of molecules from their sequences. It isn’t limited to single protein chains: It can fold multi-chain protein complexes, protein–nucleic acid assemblies, and protein–ligand complexes in one prediction. Attribute Details Developer OpenFold Consortium / AlQuraishi Lab, Columbia University Model type All-atom biomolecular structure prediction Inputs Protein, DNA, and RNA sequences. Small-molecule ligands as SMILES Outputs Predicted structures in mmCIF format, with confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, PDE) Version OpenFold3 0.4.1, of3-p2-155k checkpoint License Apache 2.0 JumpStart model ID huggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3 Supported instances ml.g6.2xlarge , ml.g6.4xlarge (default), ml.g6.12xlarge The OpenFold3 developers release its code and model weights under the Apache 2.0 license, and they publish the training data and methods. Research organizations and pharmaceutical companies can inspect the model, fine-tune it, and build on it under the terms of that license. The developers describe OpenFold3-preview as a research preview. Use cases Target and complex structure prediction – Predict structures for targets that have no experimental structure, including multi-chain assemblies and protein–nucleic acid complexes. Protein–ligand co-folding – Fold a protein together with a small molecule supplied as SMILES to generate binding-pose hypotheses for structure-based design. Antibody and protein engineering – Evaluate designed variants by predicting their structures and comparing confidence across candidates. High-throughput screening pipelines – Queue large batches of prediction jobs against an autoscaling endpoint and process the results directly from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A real-time endpoint returns its response within a single request, and that request is capped at 60 seconds. Structure prediction works differently. title: Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot
abstract: Speech-to-text inference is computationally intensive. Each audio file triggers a pipeline of deep learning models (acoustic models, language models, and post-processing stages) running on NVIDIA GPUs to meet latency requirements. At scale, this means thousands of GPU instances running continuously. AssemblyAI needed a way to run GPU-intensive inference workloads cost-effectively at scale, without sacrificing the availability and latency guarantees their customers depend on. Running entirely on On-Demand Instances would be cost-prohibitive. Spot Instances offer significant savings, while Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. AssemblyAI needed an architecture that absorbs Spot interruptions gracefully while maintaining service level agreement (SLA) commitments. Additionally, customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, finance, and legal, must keep audio data within specific geographic boundaries. They implement strict data residency configurations in European AWS Regions. Available on AWS Marketplace , AssemblyAI provides an API for transcription, speaker detection, sentiment analysis, chapter detection, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction. Their models transcribe and analyze speech for high-volume workloads across industries including technology, media, healthcare, and financial services. In this post, we show you how AssemblyAI runs cost-optimized AI inference at scale for their speech-to-text platform. The architecture uses Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Spot Instances, and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Together, these services combine a flexible fleet of NVIDIA GPUs, ECS capacity providers, and a queue-based retry mechanism. The result is significant cost savings while maintaining SLA commitments across European AWS Regions. Solution overview AssemblyAI’s inference platform runs on Amazon ECS with compute capacity managed through ECS capacity providers. The fleet mixes Amazon EC2 Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances across multiple NVIDIA GPU instance families, running a single inference model per GPU at a scale of thousands of instances. The architecture is built on four pillars that work together to deliver cost-optimized and resilient inference: Amazon ECS capacity providers mixing Spot and On-Demand. Multi-family GPU Spot diversification across EC2 instance types (such as g4dn.xlarge, g4dn.2xlarge, g5.xlarge, g5.4xlarge, and g6.2xlarge). Queue-based retry architecture using Amazon SQS for interruption recovery. Regional deployment across US West (Oregon) us-west-2 and Europe (London) eu-west-2 for data residency compliance. The following diagram illustrates how this solution is deployed: Figure 1: AssemblyAI’s inference architecture on Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 Spot GPU instances and an Amazon SQS-based retry mechanism An Amazon ECS cluster runs within a virtual private cloud (VPC) across multiple Availability Zones. The cluster hosts GPU-backed ECS tasks (shown as ECS Task, GPU Spot 1 and ECS Task GPU Spot 2) that poll the queue and process inference jobs. Each task retrieves audio files from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and writes the completed transcription to a results store, which AssemblyAI configures to deliver the output to the end customer. When a Spot Instance receives an interruption notice, Amazon EventBridge invokes the Spot Interruption Handler (an AWS Lambda function). The handler returns the in-flight job to the Main Job SQS Queue so another healthy ECS task can pick it up. Customers configure their system to route jobs that exhaust retry attempts to a Dead Letter SQS Queue for investigation. Amazon CloudWatch Metrics monitors the health of the fleet and the Spot interruption events, providing observability across the system. title: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Amazon Bedrock provides built-in, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it. The identity flows along with organizational tags, into AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) and AWS Cost Explorer while keeping data inside the AWS security boundary. This post shows you how to use these capabilities to answer three questions that every FinOps and AI Platform leader asks as AI tool adoption scales: What is the real per-user cost? Which teams generate the most spend, and does that spend correlate with the value they deliver? How should next year’s budget scale with headcount and adoption? The approach works identically regardless of which AI coding or productivity tool makes the call. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode all invoke Amazon Bedrock through one of two inference endpoints: bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle , and Bedrock’s attribution mechanism operates at the endpoint layer, beneath any tool-specific logic. You configure identity propagation once, and every tool that routes inference through Bedrock inherits per-user cost visibility automatically. By the end of this post, you will have AWS IAM Identity Center configured with your external identity provider for per-user attribution, session tags (team, cost center) flowing into CUR 2.0, Amazon Athena queries and dashboard options for ongoing cost visibility, and a clear understanding of Bedrock-native usage controls to enforce spending limits. How Amazon Bedrock attribution works Amazon Bedrock records the IAM identity of every inference caller with no changes required to your API calls. When a user invokes a model through either the bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle endpoint, Bedrock captures the caller’s full IAM ARN, including the session name for federated users and publishes it to CUR 2.0 in the line_item_iam_principal column. In billing data, usage is aggregated per principal and per usage type for each export interval: one hour in an hourly export, one day in a daily export. CUR does not contain per-request cost. For per-prompt detail, use model invocation logs or request metadata tagging. Optionally, you can attach tags to IAM principals or pass session tags during federation to add organizational dimensions. These tags appear in CUR 2.0 with the iamPrincipal/ prefix and in Cost Explorer as filterable dimensions. The mechanism supports four access patterns: IAM users, per-application roles, federated identities, and large language model (LLM) gateways proxying to Bedrock. For a comparison of all four, see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock . This post follows the federated identity pattern, which is the natural fit for AI coding and productivity tools where each developer or knowledge worker authenticates individually. Amazon Bedrock offers additional attribution mechanisms beyond IAM principal tracking that organizations can layer depending on their needs (see Appendix A for a comparison). With Application Inference Profiles, you can tag spend by workload on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. With Projects and Workspaces, you can isolate and tag spend on the bedrock-mantle endpoint. Per-request metadata tagging provides per-prompt token-level detail in model invocation logs for workloads that need granularity finer than finer than CUR 2.0’s per-usage-type aggregation per export interval. You can combine these, for example, IAM principal attribution for per-user dollars on your invoice alongside per-request metadata tags for per-prompt detail in logs. The choice depends on your goal (see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock ). The attribution problem The developer and productivity tools run on each user’s machine and call Amazon Bedrock directly, or through an LLM gateway. title: Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture
abstract: Foundation models deployed on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod meet inputs that no pre-curated dataset covers: domain-specific jargon, unexpected formats, new products, and changing user behavior. Without a record of production inference data, teams can’t detect drift, find failure patterns, or use real interactions to improve the model. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now provides Data Capture, a built-in capability that records live inference inputs and outputs to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at three independent tiers, with minimal latency impact and zero impact on model availability. In this post, we walk through one complete example on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster. A home-appliance support router captures its production traffic, Amazon Athena queries surface a new-product blind spot, a SQL policy labels the captured records, and a fine-tune on that data teaches the router the new product. We measure accuracy before and after, on data that could not have existed before the model was deployed. The inference operator serves the model on one node, and the training operator runs the fine-tuning on another. We use synthetic data for the walkthrough. The scripts, manifests, SQL, synthetic datasets, and expected outputs are available in the accompanying GitHub repository . Three-tier Data Capture architecture HyperPod Data Capture provides three independent tiers, each at a different point in the request path. You can turn on any combination in the same dataCapture block. Tier 1: SageMaker endpoint Tier 2: Load balancer Tier 3: Model pod What’s captured Full request/response payloads Application Load Balancer (ALB) access-log fields: request line, status codes, timings, client IP, user agent Full request/response payloads plus event metadata Managed by SageMaker native data capture ALB access logs HyperPod inference operator (NGINX + OTel collector + S3 uploader sidecars) Best for Compliance, Model Monitor, audit Traffic and error-rate monitoring at low cost Debugging, analytics, training-data collection Configuration sagemakerEndpoint: — sampling %, input/output, AWS KMS loadBalancer: { enabled: true } modelPod: — sampling %, input/output, buffer, max payload size, AWS KMS, content types Tiers 1 and 3 both store full payloads, so enabling both stores every record twice. Use Tier 1 for compliance and Model Monitor, Tier 2 when you only need traffic metadata, and Tier 3 when you intend to use the payloads. This post uses Tier 3 only. Because Tier 3 records complete payloads, which can include names, addresses, and order numbers, protect that data before it becomes training data. Use sampling, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption ( kmsKeyId ), S3 lifecycle rules, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction (for example, with Amazon Comprehend). Prerequisites A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), with the inference operator installed ( Setting up your HyperPod clusters for model deployment ) and the training operator EKS add-on amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-training-operator installed ( Installing the training operator ). Two available NVIDIA GPUs , one for serving and one for training. We used an ml.g6e.8xlarge for serving and an ml.g6e.xlarge for training (one 48 GB NVIDIA L40S each). title: Deploy frontier AI models on AWS Trainium with SGLang-Neuron
abstract: Today, Amazon announced that SGLang-Neuron is publicly available and can be accessed through an AWS Deep Learning Container, released by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs. With SGLang-Neuron, you can serve models and generate reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts with SGLang on AWS Trainium using the same SGLang interface you use today. Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers strong economics for AI training and inference at scale. Now, running SGLang on Trainium follows the SGLang workflow you already know: you launch models through SGLang’s server interface and invoke the endpoint using the same generation APIs. Underneath that interface, SGLang-Neuron runs on native PyTorch. With its out-of-tree plugin design, Trainium support and SGLang core develop independently and iterate faster. How SGLang runs on Trainium SGLang-Neuron is an out-of-tree plugin that connects SGLang with AWS Trainium. Installing the plugin registers the neuron platform through SGLang’s plugin entry points, and setting SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron selects it when the server starts. SGLang core continues to provide the API server, request lifecycle, RadixAttention, and prefix-cache bookkeeping. The plugin implements the Trainium-specific models, attention, mixture of experts (MoE), and the graph runner. Figure 1: SGLang-Neuron on AWS Trainium TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device. SGLang-Neuron uses standard PyTorch operations for the model execution path and incorporates kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for performance. It compiles these operations and kernels into executable programs using torch.compile , which the graph runner prepares and executes during serving. SGLang-Neuron also supports PD disaggregation . In this configuration, a prefill server computes the prompt KV cache and transfers it to a decode server using NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) . The decode server then generates the remaining tokens. Each server still uses SGLang’s scheduler and request lifecycle, while the plugin manages the Trainium execution and KV-cache transfer path. title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: At Natera , a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations. This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows. SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives. The challenge: Knowledge continuity Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale. With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop. Why Natera chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision: Autonomous processing of high-volume support tickets without human intervention. Deep integration with existing operational tools such as Jira and Confluence. Built-in security and observability (encryption, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration, and distributed tracing) without requiring the team to build and maintain custom infrastructure. “We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said. AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB , a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) , and AWS X-Ray , a capability of Amazon CloudWatch. How SWARM works: Two agents, one skill library SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths. “The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said. Four layers connect the architecture: The event layer routes Jira tickets through Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS. The agent layer hosts swarm-agent, swarm-hive, and the skill library, and delivers diagnostic reports back to engineers. The context layer draws on vendor manuals, historical tickets, and operational data. The observability and delivery layer captures traces, logs, and metrics. title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
abstract: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching . For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance . For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock . Where inference cost comes from Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Prompt cache duration Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching , which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: { "cachePoint": { "type": "default", "ttl": "1h" } } For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control . A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times. These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour. Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout. Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference. Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. abstract: Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock , we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center , Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs , and AWS Lambda . This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate. This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution , which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed. Solution overview The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce. Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role , for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough. Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries. Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed. Permissions to tag IAM principal , activate cost allocation tags , create data exports , and create budgets and budget actions. Amazon Bedrock accessed through IAM roles or IAM users. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with appropriate credentials. A CUR 2.0 data export and an Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ) bucket to receive it. title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent. This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions. In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership. Cost per task, not cost per token Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes. The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering. None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page . The four hidden cost drivers Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload. Tokenizer efficiency A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’s list price is 15 percent lower but its tokenizer needs 40 percent more tokens for your data (common with structured schemas and numerical arrays), Model B is cheaper. The gap widens for non-English text: many tokenizers fragment non-Latin scripts into two to three times more tokens than the equivalent English. Output alignment and verbosity Output tokens commonly cost 3–5x more than input tokens (the ratio varies by family. Refer to the Bedrock pricing page ). A model that ignores formatting constraints like “return only raw JSON” makes you pay that output premium for filler words. A model that follows formatting instructions closely saves money by generating fewer of these more expensive output tokens. Agentic loop efficiency Agentic workflows change the cost math entirely. Tool use (function calling) lets a model invoke external functions, requiring a multi-turn loop: analyze the prompt, decide to call a tool, wait for the observation, generate an answer. Each turn re-sends the full conversation history and tool results as input tokens. A model that takes four turns (each one re-sending a larger context payload) costs far more than one that finishes in a single pass. Reasoning overhead Many models support extended thinking , working through a chain of thought before the visible answer. Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens, so a model that thinks for 2,000 tokens before a 200-token answer bills you for 2,200. Some models redact the reasoning while still charging for it. abstract: Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants. In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. abstract: AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months ( METR ), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago ( McKinsey ). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments. Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable. The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents ( Deloitte ). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one. abstract: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock , you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base . Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS . The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. Why move to Managed Knowledge Base We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost. AWS runs the store With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model. Built-in capabilities Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself: Native connectors ingest content directly from sources such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence. For the current list, see supported connectors . After the first full sync, later syncs pick up only changes, on demand or on a schedule. The Managed Knowledge Base includes a deletion safeguard to help protect against accidental bulk removal of indexed content. For connectors that support it, such as Microsoft SharePoint and Atlassian Confluence, a real-time check against the source also catches permission changes since the last sync. ACL awareness doesn’t authenticate users, so your application must verify and pass the user’s identity. Agentic retrieval answers questions that a single search can’t by handling multi-part questions and retrieving iteratively. It can search more than one knowledge base in a single request. title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
abstract: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project , and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A , we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions. Solution overview Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider. Figure 1: A2A agents across an enterprise account and a SaaS provider account During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared. After onboarding, each request follows these steps: The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool. title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
abstract: More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see? Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base. Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee. In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. On top of that, we add independent layers of defense in case that mechanism has a bug or is bypassed. Solution overview Managed Knowledge Base has a feature called ACL awareness . When a search request includes a user context ( userContext ) with the user’s email in userId , the knowledge base returns only the documents that user is allowed to view. If your application calls the search API directly, the application code sets the search scope from the authentication result. Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base shows this pattern. When you expose the knowledge base as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway, however, userContext becomes a tool argument, and the LLM constructs its value. Neither the gateway nor the knowledge base verifies that this value belongs to the authenticated user. This solution injects verified user attributes into tool calls at the tool layer (AgentCore Gateway). It then scopes the search by those attributes at the resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base). The sample stores three documents in a single knowledge base: business plans for department A and department B, and a notice shared with all departments. title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
abstract: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “ Is this agent ready for production? ” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. 1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
abstract: Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore . We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together. Prerequisites To follow along with this walkthrough, you need the following: Java – JDK 21 (required) Spring Boot – 4.1 (with Spring AI 2.0 and spring-ai-agentcore 2.0) Maven – 3.9+. Node.js – 18+ (for the React frontend) Terraform – 1.5+. Docker – with Buildx for multi-architecture builds. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) – v2, configured with credentials. An AWS account . What makes a system an agent A chat completion call can generate text, but it can’t decide what to do next, reach into external systems, or remember what happened yesterday. An agent can, because it unites three capabilities: Planning – Given a goal, the model breaks it into steps, prioritizes them, and revises the plan as new information arrives. Tool use – Beyond generating text, the model can select and invoke external functions such as APIs, databases, and code interpreters to act in the world. Memory – Context carries across turns (short-term) and across sessions (long-term), so each decision builds on what came before. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application has limited tool use (retrieval) but no planning loop. An agent has all three, operating in a goal-directed loop until the task is complete or it determines it cannot proceed. The following diagram shows these capabilities in an end-to-end agentic pipeline, from request to grounded answer. Figure 1: Agentic reference architecture. A request flows through the runtime, guardrails, classification, a specialist agent, tools, the foundation model, memory, rules, and human review to a grounded answer, with resilience and observability as cross-cutting concerns The pipeline has 11 stages. A client submits a document and question. The request passes through a runtime gateway for authentication and rate limiting, then input guardrails screen for harmful content. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined developments from OpenAI and Anthropic, the growing push for regional AI models, and the challenges of making AI more accessible and responsible. Frontier AI is moving into everyday services OpenAI introduced LifeVal , a benchmark that measures how well AI handles everyday tasks such as finding childcare, managing household budgets, and accessing government services. Meanwhile, Anthropic began testing read-only banking connections in Claude , allowing some US subscribers to analyze spending and identify unusual charges. Separately, nonprofit research organization METR reported that AI assistance may have roughly doubled the pace of progress on certain model development tasks at Anthropic over the past year. That makes it increasingly important to understand how AI is shaping that progress and to check the reliability of the outputs these systems produce. title: What Makes an Agent Self-Evolving?
abstract: An agent can get better at its job without a new model. It can learn to find useful information, choose the right tool, or check that a task is finished before reporting success. For that experience to help with the next task, something has to carry over: an updated instruction, a lesson saved in memory, or a change to the software that runs the agent. That is what interests me about a self-evolving agent: It can use experience to change how it handles future tasks. Much of that change happens in the harness , the instructions, context, tools, and software around the model. Research such as Harness-RSI explores how agents can change that harness while continuing to use the same model. Of course, a change can make things worse. A saved memory might be wrong, or a new instruction might fix one problem and create another. I think about self-evolving agents in three parts: evaluation to tell whether a change helped, an improvement process that can do more of the work on its own, and the parts of the harness it is allowed to change. Evaluation: What counts as improvement? Before I ask an agent to improve itself, I want to know what doing a better job would look like. A model’s score on a benchmark tells us how it performed on that test. To evaluate an agent built with that model, we also need to ask whether it used the right information, took the right actions, and met the user’s requirements. In a restaurant-planning exercise I developed for teaching evaluation, an agent is given a group’s needs and information about restaurants. Its job is to suggest a place and a time for dinner. The people and restaurants are fictional, but success is easy to understand: Can everyone eat there, afford it, and make it on time? In one test, the agent recommended a restaurant that met everyone’s needs. My evaluation still marked the answer as wrong because it compared the wording with a sample answer I had written. But my answer was only one possible solution. A different recommendation could work just as well. That feedback could lead a self-improving agent to “fix” a decision that was already good. A more useful evaluation would check whether the recommendation met the group’s requirements. If someone’s budget is $25 and the meal costs $28, the plan fails that check. We can build a custom evaluation around those requirements, checking the price, dietary needs, and timing. Other questions require judgment, such as whether the agent clearly explained a trade-off between price and convenience. A person or another model can help assess those. If we asked the agent to make a booking as well, we would need to check that the reservation actually existed. A message saying, “Your table is booked” would not be enough. Evaluating the system means checking what it did, as well as what it said. Once the agent proposes a change, we can test the updated version against the current one. It should still handle tasks it already did well. We should also try cases that were not used to develop or choose the change. Getting one dinner plan right tells us less than handling new groups with different budgets, dietary needs, and schedules. The evaluation should also explain why an answer failed. “The meal costs more than the guest’s budget” gives the agent something specific to investigate. It still needs to find the cause, but it knows where to start. Autonomous improvement: Who carries the work forward? If an engineer has to spot every failure, suggest every change, and start every test, improvement still depends on that person. Autonomous improvement means giving more of this work to the system. It can review past tasks, look for repeated mistakes, propose a change, and test whether the change helps. For example, a more autonomous dinner planner might notice that it repeatedly recommended restaurants people could not afford, even though their budgets were available. abstract: This post was created with the assistance of AI, based on a transcript of the conversation. AI tools have started to remember their users, but each tool remembers a different version of the same person. Duncan Davidson, an independent consultant and longtime software engineer, has been trying to connect those fragments. He joined Ben Lorica to discuss what personal AI could do if people could carry their context between services and decide what each service gets to see. They also talked about how AI coding changed web development during Duncan’s time at Webflow, what new developers may lose as entry-level work changes, and why open source projects need new ways to handle AI-assisted contributions. About the Generative AI in the Real World podcast: In 2023, ChatGPT put AI on everyone’s agenda. In 2026, the challenge will be turning those agendas into reality. In Generative AI in the Real World , Ben Lorica interviews leaders who are building with AI. Learn from their experience to help put AI to work in your enterprise. Duncan compared AI coding to desktop publishing, which removed the physical work of assembling pages but left designers responsible for what the page should look like. At Webflow, he saw people use AI tools to make websites faster than they could with earlier tools. For developers, he said, the question has shifted from how quickly they can type code to “What outcome do you want? What are you trying to do with this code, and how can you make it better?” People still need to judge whether an implementation fits the rest of the system. 10.41 New developers still need a way to become experts. Computer science fundamentals still matter when an agent offers several plausible fixes and a person must choose the one that fits a larger system. Ben asked where future engineers will gain that judgment if AI absorbs entry-level tasks. title: Why Git Needs Help: Moving from Files to Systems for Source Control
abstract: The shift to agentic reality When Git was designed in 2005, Linus Torvalds solved a brilliant problem for humans collaborating over terminal windows by trading line-by-line diffs. Fast-forward to 2026: Autonomous coding agents don’t think in flat text files or line breaks. They reason across syntax trees, execution traces, call graphs, and type constraints. In my view, forcing an AI agent to engineer complex distributed systems through string matching is like handing a chief software architect a chisel and a stack of sticky notes. File-centric versus system-centric paradigm shift Dimension Legacy file-centric (Git) Agent-native system graph Representation Flat Unicode text streams Tree-Sitter ASTs & CPG nodes Mutation unit Line-by-line string diffs AST node transformations Context overhead 2,000+ line prompt context fills Sub-50 token targeted node payloads State persistence Ephemeral model prompt windows Execution ledgers & reasoning chains Whenever I see engineers try to lock context-blind models into file-centric version control, I watch the consequences compound quickly. Context windows fill with irrelevant churn, API bills surge, and subtle, multifile structural breakages slip past basic syntax checks. Just as critically, standard Git discards the cognitive history of a change. The moment an agent session completes, its execution logs, compiler feedback, and discarded hypotheses evaporate into thin air. Tactical illustration: renaming a distributed method signature Consider updating a core helper signature across 40 dependent services. A traditional string diff forces the agent to read and mutate thousands of lines of surrounding boilerplate text, burning thousands of context tokens per file: --- a/services/auth.py +++ b/services/auth.py @@ -42,7 +42,7 @@ class AuthManager: def validate_session(self, token: str) -> UserSession: - return fetch_user_by_token(token) + return fetch_user_by_token(token, include_metadata=True) In contrast, an AST mutation node isolates the target function symbol, executing the change precisely without passing unneeded ambient text through the prompt window: { "action": "mutate_node", "target_ast_id": "ast_node_89f2a41b", "symbol": "fetch_user_by_token", "update": { "add_argument": { "name": "include_metadata", "value": true } } } This exact bottleneck hit Anthropic in late 2026. As autonomous agent activity pushed monorepo merges beyond 30,000 per day, conventional Git infrastructure simply buckled under the load. To me, unlocking genuine agentic autonomy requires evolving source control along two complementary tracks: shifting to server-hosted, graph-aware architectures, and treating agent reasoning as a first-class, versioned artifact right alongside the code itself. Why text diffs and ephemeral sessions create silent debt Standard diff tools operate purely on raw Unicode strings. When an agent reorders functions or cleans up formatting, string diffs pollute context windows with noise while remaining blind to structural reality. If you modify a single method signature, Git won’t warn you about the dozen callers broken across separate modules. From my experience, feeding 2,000-line source files into prompts just to update a 5-line helper method degrades model attention, burns compute, and inflates overhead at scale. Text diffs versus AST graph mutations Metric / behavior Text diff (unified patch) AST graph mutation Formatting resilience Breaks on whitespace or line-ending changes Immune to syntax formatting shifts Impact analysis Post hoc CI test failures Sub-second static call-graph resolution Token consumption O(file_size) per prompt iteration O(node_delta) per targeted change Compounding this structural blind spot is what I consider our biggest waste: ephemeral session memory. Whenever an agent finishes a task or compacts its context window, its entire diagnostic history—failed attempts, shell outputs, and compiler warnings—disappears. title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
abstract: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it . The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough . Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy. The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however. The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants. Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data.
